title: Overfitting, Underfitting, and Regularization
learningObjectives: Diagnose overfitting and underfitting from training and validation behavior.
Explain regularization and common generalization remedies.
Choose remedies based on evidence rather than habit.

mentalModel.text: A model should learn repeatable patterns, not memorize examples. Underfitting means it has not captured enough useful structure. Overfitting means it learned training-specific details that do not carry over to unseen examples.

concepts.title: Technical deep dive and worked example

blocks.text: Regularization discourages overly complex fits. L2 penalizes squared parameter magnitudes; L1 penalizes absolute magnitudes and can set weights to zero. Early stopping selects a checkpoint based on validation behavior.

blocks.problem: Training accuracy rises from 92% to 99%, while validation accuracy peaks at 90% and then falls to 84%.
reasoning: Check split integrity, duplicates, and distribution mismatch first.
If the evaluation is sound, choose the checkpoint near the best validation score.
Try stronger regularization, a simpler model, label-preserving augmentation, or more representative data.
Compare changes on the same validation protocol; keep the final test set untouched.
blocks.outcome: The best model is not necessarily the one with the highest training score or longest training run.

blocks.title: How regularization changes the objective

blocks.text: Expected output: Increasing lambda makes large weights more costly. Too little may not control overfitting; too much can force the model to underfit.
Regularization can improve generalization but excessive strength underfits. Larger models may need more data and compute. Augmentation helps only when the transformation preserves the target.
Production check: Track train/validation gaps and performance by user group or region. A good validation score can still fail after a distribution shift.

blocks.title: Anti-pattern to avoid
blocks.content: Adding dropout to every model without evidence; training longer because training accuracy rises; treating one validation curve as proof without checking the split.

blocks.text: 1. Problem and motivation — Training accuracy can keep rising while real-world performance falls. Learning curves help distinguish a model that is too limited from one that is fitting noise.

2. Definition and design choice — Regularization discourages overly complex fits. L2 penalizes squared parameter magnitudes; L1 penalizes absolute magnitudes and can set weights to zero. Early stopping selects a checkpoint based on validation behavior.

3. Internal mechanism — Compare training and validation curves, choose checkpoints based on validation, and test remedies such as regularization, augmentation, simpler models, or more representative data.

blocks.text: 4. Trade-offs and scale — Regularization can improve generalization but excessive strength underfits. Larger models may need more data and compute. Augmentation helps only when the transformation preserves the target.
5. Anti-patterns — Adding dropout to every model without evidence; training longer because training accuracy rises; treating one validation curve as proof without checking the split.
6. Interview probes — How do train and validation curves differ? What does lambda control? When would you add data instead of reducing model size? How do you avoid tuning on test?

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.title: Engineering rule of thumb
tradeoffsAndPitfalls.content: Select the best generalizing model, not the model that memorizes the training set best.

questions.prompt: Which pattern most strongly suggests overfitting?

options.text: Both training and validation errors are high
Training error is low but validation error is much higher
Both metrics are strong and close

questions.explanation: A large generalization gap suggests the model has fit training-specific patterns.

questions.prompt: Training and validation performance are both poor. What is a reasonable hypothesis?

options.text: Underfitting, weak features, or a poor training setup

questions.explanation: Poor performance on both partitions can indicate insufficient signal or model fit, though data problems must also be checked.

questions.prompt: What does an L2 penalty encourage?

options.text: Smaller parameter magnitudes by penalizing squared weights

questions.explanation: L2 adds a penalty related to squared parameter values.

options.text: Choose a checkpoint near the best validation behavior

questions.explanation: Early stopping uses validation behavior to select a checkpoint.

questions.prompt: Increasing regularization always improves model quality.
questions.explanation: Too much regularization can make a model underfit.

questions.prompt: The model with the highest training accuracy is always the model to deploy.
questions.explanation: Selection should consider validation performance and final test evidence, not training accuracy alone.

interviewScenarios.prompt: A model has 99% training accuracy and 82% validation accuracy. Outline a disciplined diagnosis.
strongAnswerPoints: Check split strategy, duplicates, leakage, and distribution differences.
Verify metric and label definitions match.
If the gap is genuine, try regularization, simpler capacity, augmentation, or more representative data.
pitfalls: Tuning repeatedly on the final test set
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: I would verify the split and labels first. If the gap is genuine, I would test a smaller model, regularization, augmentation, and better data against the same validation set, reserving the final test for the final estimate.

interviewScenarios.prompt: Both training and validation errors are high. What would you investigate before increasing model size?
strongAnswerPoints: Check label quality and feature signal.
Compare with a simple baseline and inspect errors.
Check optimization and convergence before adding capacity.
pitfalls: Assuming every weak model needs more parameters
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: I would compare against a baseline, inspect labels and features, and check whether training converged. High errors in both sets can reflect weak data or a mismatched objective, not just insufficient capacity.
